Intersectionality. The analytical framework recognizing that social identities and oppressions—race, gender, class, sexuality, disability—do not operate in isolation but interact and reinforce one another. Emerging from Black feminist theory and articulated forcefully by thinkers like bell hooks, intersectionality reveals how power structures compound, requiring analysis and activism that addresses multiple overlapping forms of marginalization. This concept has become foundational to contemporary social justice movements worldwide. Intersectionality is rooted in the recognition that Black women and women of color face distinct oppressions that cannot be separated into isolated categories. Their experiences are qualitatively different from white women's or Black men's experiences. The framework was articulated through Sojourner Truth's famous testimony "Ain't I a Woman?" in eighteen fifty-one, which interrogated assumptions about womanhood across racial lines by pointing out that enslaved Black women were denied the protections supposedly granted to all women—decades before the framework had a name. Intersectionality was formalized as an academic framework in the late twentieth century by scholars including Kimberlé Crenshaw, who coined the term in nineteen eighty-nine, Patricia Hill Collins, and bell hooks, drawing on decades of Black feminist thought in the civil rights and Black Power eras. A Black woman's experience is not simply the sum of racism plus sexism, but a unique intersection producing distinct realities. She faces discrimination and barriers that white women don't face and that Black men don't face. Intersectionality applies to understanding discrimination and privilege by recognizing that an individual may hold power in one dimension—class or sexuality—while experiencing marginalization in another—race or disability. Power is not distributed uniformly across social locations. Intersectionality is central to modern feminism, activism, and policy-making. It reveals why one-size-fits-all solutions fail, why mainstream feminism excluding women of color has limitations, and why movements must address interconnected oppressions simultaneously. The framework extends beyond gender and race to encompass disability, sexuality, immigration status, age, religion, and other dimensions of identity and power, recognizing that oppression is multidimensional and that liberation requires addressing all systems of domination.
